questions.stem: Which pair names the two forces on any falling object?

options.explanation: No engine acts on a freely falling body.
The downward weight and the upward air resistance — the pair of record.
Neither acts in free fall through air.
No surface touches the object, so no reaction acts.

questions.stem: As a falling object's speed increases, the air resistance on it:

options.explanation: The opposite: drag grows with speed.
Only the weight is constant; drag is speed-sensitive.

options.text: Falls to zero at high speed
options.explanation: Nothing zeroes the drag.
More speed means more collisions with air particles — more drag.

questions.stem: During the whole fall, the object's weight:

options.explanation: W = m × g with both factors fixed: the weight never changes.
That is the drag's habit, not the weight's.

options.text: Falls to zero at terminal velocity
options.explanation: The weight persists; the resultant is what zeroes.
The weight points downward throughout.

questions.stem: Why does faster falling mean larger air resistance?

options.text: The air thickens with altitude changes
options.explanation: Air density is not the mechanism of record.
Weight stays fixed.

options.text: More air particles are struck each second
options.explanation: Drag comes from collisions; speed raises the collision rate.
Gravity is independent of the fall's speed.

questions.stem: At the instant a skydiver steps from the plane, before falling, the resultant force on them is:

options.text: Zero, because they are momentarily still
options.explanation: Stillness does not zero the forces; only weight acts and it is unopposed.

options.text: Equal to the weight, directed downward
options.explanation: With no support and no drag yet, the weight is the whole resultant.

options.text: Equal to the drag, directed upward
options.explanation: The drag is essentially zero at that instant.
Nothing pushes the diver upward.

questions.stem: Name the two forces acting on a falling object, with their directions.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight, acting downward, and air resistance — a drag force — acting upward.

questions.stem: State why the weight of the falling object does not change.
questions.modelAnswer: Because W = m × g and neither the mass nor the freefall acceleration changes during the fall.

questions.stem: Explain why air resistance grows as the object speeds up.
questions.modelAnswer: The drag comes from collisions between the object and air particles. A faster object meets more particles every second, so the opposing force grows with the speed.

questions.stem: A 700 N skydiver feels 250 N of drag at one instant of the fall. Give the size and direction of the resultant force.
questions.modelAnswer: 700 − 250 = 450 N, directed downward — the weight still outpaces the drag at that instant.

questions.stem: Terminal velocity is reached at the instant when:

options.text: The weight has worn away to nothing
options.explanation: The weight never fades; the drag rises to meet it.
Zero drag is the release instant, not the balance.

options.text: The drag has grown to equal the weight
options.explanation: Equality of the two forces is the balance condition.
The balance happens in mid-fall.

questions.stem: At terminal velocity, the object's acceleration is:

options.explanation: Zero resultant means no further acceleration.
The maximum belongs to the release instant.
Nothing grows at balance; everything is steady.
g applies only while the weight is unopposed.

questions.stem: How does the skydiver's acceleration behave across the whole fall?

options.explanation: The resultant shrinks; so does the acceleration.
Only the first instant carries the full g.
Nothing reverses; it decays to zero.

options.text: It is largest at release and decreases to zero
options.explanation: Weight-minus-drag shrinks as drag builds — the acceleration decays with it.

questions.stem: Once terminal velocity is reached, the object's speed is:

options.explanation: A zero resultant leaves nothing to rise with.

options.text: Constant at its maximum for the fall
options.explanation: Terminal velocity is the steady fastest speed.
The balance holds the speed steady.
No oscillation appears in the law of record.

questions.stem: A skydiver whose weight is 700 N has reached terminal velocity. The drag on them is:

options.explanation: Balance means drag equals weight exactly.
Less would leave a resultant and further acceleration.
Zero drag was the start, not the balance.
Nothing doubles the forces here.

questions.modelAnswer: The fastest speed a falling object reaches, held constant once the drag has grown to balance the weight.

questions.stem: State the value of the resultant force at terminal velocity.
questions.modelAnswer: Zero — the upward and downward forces are balanced exactly.

questions.stem: Explain, stage by stage, why the skydiver's acceleration falls from its initial maximum to zero.
questions.modelAnswer: At release only the weight acts, so the resultant — and the acceleration — is at maximum. As speed builds, the drag grows and the resultant (weight minus drag) shrinks, so the acceleration decreases. When the drag equals the weight the resultant reaches zero, and the speed stops changing: terminal velocity.

questions.stem: Mid-fall, a 700 N skydiver feels 250 N of drag. Later, the drag has reached 700 N. Describe the motion in the later instant.
questions.modelAnswer: With drag equal to the 700 N weight, the resultant is zero: acceleration has ended, and the pace holds steady at the terminal value.
